method: Sequential fresh processes on shared workstation; fixed real M6 FK/Jacobian and CartesianServo for both arms; same 0.005s dt, fixed 3/2/1mm displacement; no accept(), no 200Hz pacing, no live transport. All modes use identical servo and stage timers. Flat numeric sample arrays avoid tracked statistics tuple growth; normal GC timed. Busy modes synthesize one CPU-bound pure-Python load and are mechanism tests, not representative measured device load. Feedback modes use actual Python receive paths with synthetic 1kHz arm packets and two synthetic hand joint/diagnostic streams each at indicated frequency. No Quest parsing, native SDK property traversal, hand retargeting, or real stop callbacks. Rates are experiment parameters, not measurements. Individual extrema/P99 with different sample sizes are not stable rankings. Both arms use 100% velocity/acceleration ratios, unlike the recorded right-arm 15% setting. Linux-only experiment uses /proc and fork. Low fixed-target QP iteration counts do not exclude difficult real target/posture cases.
script_note: Docstring was expanded during execution to state Linux-only and arm-ratio limitations; executable statements did not change.
conclusion: A controlled pure-Python CPU burner in the same process causally inflated servo wall time while thread CPU time remained low; moving the identical load into another process removed most of that inflation despite the burner consuming a full CPU. Busy-stage medians near the 5ms GIL switch interval, no other kinematics lock user, and fast CPU times support GIL reacquisition as the mechanism in this synthetic test. This does not establish the actual robot process had equivalent CPU/GIL load. Synthetic feedback at 200Hz reduced load relative to 1kHz, but did not produce a hard real-time guarantee. Shorter GIL interval and one BLAS thread did not improve tail latency in these sequential shared-workstation runs; no production tuning is justified from this experiment alone.
